alt: Line chart of clock time per test case against computing time per case. At 8 CPUs clock time equals computing time from 12 to 28 s. At 4 CPUs 12 s of computing takes 24 s and 14 s takes 28 s; 16, 20, 24 and 28 s are marked as timed out at the 30 s limit, with 48 of 50 cases timed out and no score. A note says the fixed checker passes the 16 s and 28 s solutions on all 50 cases with 19.80 out of 100.
caption: On EdgeBench's official 4-CPU setting, a valid Grid Turing Robot solution that needs more than about 15 s of computing per test case gets no score, although the instructions promise 30 s per case. The agent writes a rule table that steers a robot over a grid; the checker runs 8 cases at once, so on 4 CPUs each case gets half a CPU and takes twice as long by the clock, and one timed-out case voids the whole submission. Test solutions needing 16 s and 28 s per case timed out on 48 of 50 cases under the original checker and scored 19.80 out of 100 under the fixed one, which runs no more cases at once than it has CPUs.
